newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage-takers agree to peace commission.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage-takers agree to peace commission.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages at the Japanese embassy in Lima accepted on Wednesday a government proposal to set up a "guarantor" committee to oversee a peaceful solution.

"The proposal to set up a committee is acceptable," Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said in a radio conversation from within the residence monitored by Reuters.
Cerpa also pledged the rebels would not "execute" any of their hostages. "It is not in our minds to carry out executions, nor to give any ultimatums," he said. "We have never spoken of executions."

He said the MRTA would accept Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and a Red Cross representative on the committee as suggested by the government. But the rebels also asked for representation from Guatemala and a European country.
"The place of the meeting is a matter that can be discussed and decided by mutual accord," he added.

Despite the apparent step forward in the 29-day crisis, the MRTA claimed real progress was impossible while the government stood fast in its refusal to discuss their chief demand: the release of all jailed comrades.
"The government proposes a peaceful solution but at the same time says it does not have anything to negotiate with us," Cerpa said. Officials have flatly refused any releases.

Cerpa warned that without tangible progress in negotiations the crisis was "being pushed towards a military end" and said the government would be to blame for any injury to hostages in a possible storming of the residence.

The rebel leader also told the government his comrades would not accept a peaceful end to the crisis involving their surrender. "The peaceful way out is not where we go out laying down our arms and giving up. That is impossible."
There was no immediate response from the government to the rebels' latest communication. "This takes time," said a source close to official negotiator Domingo Palermo.

The MRTA statement on the commission was the first move in negotiations since the cancellation on Sunday of a planned face-to-face meeting between Cerpa and government negotiator Domingo Palermo. That fell through because the MRTA wanted the release of their comrades to be discussed at the meeting.

But the Japanese government cautiously welcomed the rebels' communication on Wednesday. "Even if I'm conservative about it, I must say it's not a bad thing. But I would not want to get carried away," said an official of the Japanese government's task force in Lima.
During and after the MRTA's communication, there was a flurry of activity at the residence, with both hostages and rebels appearing at the windows.
A relaxed-looking captive Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela was seen talking into a radio, while a rebel girl holding a gun waved at photographers on a nearby roof.

Cerpa, who denied claims the rebels wanted ransom money for the Japanese businessmen among the hostages, said the MRTA was handling its captives with "a treatment respectful of their dignity as people."
The rebels initially took more than 500 hostages but have released most as "goodwill gestures," keeping the 74 men they consider their most valuable bargaining chips.

President Alberto Fujimori returned to the grim reality of the siege Wednesday after two days of distractions offered by the visit of Ecuador's leader Abdala Bucaram. Fujimori raced around Lima and the provinces with Bucaram on Tuesday, winning support from cheering crowds and praise from Ecuador's president for his tough line with the rebels.

Cipriani, a close friend of the president and named by the Vatican to sit on the proposed guarantor commission, travelled with Fujimori and called on all sides to sit down for talks as soon as possible.

In an internet communique, the MRTA called for supporters around the world to join their cause. "It is necessary to put pressure on Fujimori to release all our political prisoner comrades, who are hostages of the dictatorial regime," it said in a statement on its "Rebel Voice" internet web page.
The MRTA proposed protests outside Peruvian embassies and consulates over the next three days and a writing campaign of letters sent to Fujimori and copied to human rights organisation and the media.
